concepts.title: Neural network basics
concepts.kw: neural networks layers neurons weights activation functions relu sigmoid backpropagation epochs dropout batch normalisation deep learning pytorch
concepts.s: A neural network stacks layers of simple units that compute weighted sums followed by non-linear activations, and learns the weights with backpropagation and gradient descent.
concepts.d: Each layer multiplies its inputs by a weight matrix, adds a bias and applies an activation function such as ReLU, which lets the network learn non-linear patterns. Stacking layers lets it learn increasingly abstract features. Training runs a forward pass to get predictions and the loss, then backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss for every weight using the chain rule, and an optimiser like Adam updates them. Overfitting is controlled with dropout, weight decay, early stopping and more data. Deep learning shines on images, text and audio, while gradient boosting usually wins on ordinary tabular data.
concepts.e: A network classifying parcel photos as damaged or intact uses convolutional layers to detect edges and creases, then dense layers to decide, reaching 94% accuracy after 10 epochs with dropout.
concepts.c: Why does a neural network need non-linear activation functions?
concepts.i: Expect to explain layers, activations, backpropagation and regularisation, and when deep learning beats tree models.

concepts.title: Embeddings
concepts.kw: embeddings vector representation semantic similarity cosine similarity word2vec sentence embeddings vector database nearest neighbour search dimensions
concepts.s: An embedding represents an item, such as a word, document, product or user, as a vector of numbers placed so that similar items are close together.
concepts.d: Embeddings are learned by models: word2vec learned word vectors from context, and modern text embedding models produce a vector for a whole sentence or document that captures its meaning. Similarity is usually measured with cosine similarity. Embeddings power semantic search, where a query finds documents with similar meaning even without matching words, as well as recommendations, clustering, deduplication and features for other models. Vector databases and libraries such as FAISS, pgvector or Pinecone store them and run fast approximate nearest-neighbour search. The same embedding model must be used for queries and documents.
concepts.e: The query "parcel arrived broken" and a support article titled "Reporting damaged deliveries" share no keywords, but their embeddings have cosine similarity 0.82, so semantic search finds the article.
concepts.c: Why can embedding search find relevant documents that keyword search misses?
concepts.i: Expect to explain what embeddings are, how similarity search works, and where they're used in data products.

concepts.title: Transformers and attention
concepts.kw: transformers attention self attention multi head attention tokens positional encoding encoder decoder bert gpt context window parallel
concepts.s: The transformer is the neural network architecture behind modern language models. Its key idea, attention, lets every token look at every other token to decide what's relevant.
concepts.d: Text is split into tokens, each mapped to an embedding plus a positional encoding so order is known. In self-attention, each token creates a query, a key and a value vector; comparing a token's query with every other token's key gives attention weights, and the output is a weighted mix of their values. Multi-head attention does this several times in parallel to capture different relationships. Stacked layers of attention and feed-forward networks build up meaning. Encoder models like BERT read the whole text and suit classification; decoder models like GPT generate text one token at a time. Attention's cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which limits context windows.
concepts.e: In "The courier picked up the parcel because it was ready", attention lets the model link "it" to "parcel" rather than "courier", based on the surrounding words.
concepts.c: Why could transformers train much faster than earlier recurrent networks?
concepts.i: Senior ML and LLM roles ask you to explain self-attention, encoder versus decoder models, and context length limits.

concepts.title: LLM fundamentals: tokens, context and sampling
concepts.kw: llm large language model tokens tokenisation context window temperature top p sampling hallucination pretraining fine tuning instruction tuning rlhf
concepts.s: Large language models predict the next token given the text so far. Understanding tokens, context windows and sampling explains both their strengths and their failures.
concepts.d: Text is split into tokens, roughly three quarters of an English word each, and both cost and limits are measured in tokens. The context window is the maximum tokens the model can consider at once, including the prompt, any documents and the answer. Models are pretrained on huge text collections to predict the next token, then instruction-tuned and aligned with human feedback to follow instructions. Generation samples one token at a time: temperature controls randomness, and top-p limits sampling to the most likely tokens. Because they generate plausible text rather than looking up facts, LLMs can hallucinate, which grounding with retrieved data reduces.
concepts.e: Summarising 200 support tickets of 300 tokens each needs about 60,000 input tokens, so it's split into batches. Temperature 0 keeps the summaries consistent across runs.
concepts.c: Why might you set temperature to 0 for extracting fields from invoices?
concepts.i: Expect to explain tokens, context windows, temperature, hallucination, and fine-tuning versus prompting.

concepts.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
concepts.kw: rag retrieval augmented generation chunking embeddings vector search hybrid search reranking grounding citations hallucination knowledge base
concepts.s: Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions by first retrieving relevant passages from your own documents or data, then asking the LLM to answer using them.
concepts.d: Documents are split into chunks, embedded and stored in a vector index. At question time, the question is embedded, the most similar chunks are retrieved, often combined with keyword search (hybrid search) and reranked, and they're placed in the prompt with instructions to answer only from them and cite sources. RAG keeps answers grounded and current without retraining the model, and lets you control access to documents. Quality depends mostly on retrieval: chunk size, metadata filters and reranking matter. Evaluate retrieval (were the right chunks found?) separately from generation (was the answer faithful to them?).
concepts.e: An internal assistant answers "What's our SLA for B2B returns?" by retrieving two policy paragraphs and replying with the 7-day SLA, citing the policy document and section.
concepts.c: Why evaluate retrieval separately from the generated answer in a RAG system?
concepts.i: Expect to design a RAG pipeline, discuss chunking and retrieval quality, and explain how you'd evaluate and reduce hallucination.

concepts.title: Prompting LLMs for data tasks
concepts.kw: prompting prompt engineering few shot examples structured output json schema text to sql extraction classification instructions system prompt
concepts.s: LLMs can classify text, extract fields, write SQL and summarise data, and clear prompts with examples and structured outputs make them reliable enough to use in pipelines.
concepts.d: Give clear instructions: the task, the context, the allowed labels or fields, and how to handle edge cases such as unknown values. Few-shot examples show the exact format and judgement you want. Ask for structured output, such as JSON matching a schema, and validate it in code. For text-to-SQL, provide the table schemas, column meanings and example queries, then run the SQL against a read-only connection and check the results. Use temperature 0 for consistency, test prompts on a labelled sample before scaling up, and track cost per record.
concepts.e: A prompt with eight labelled examples classifies customer complaints into 6 categories as JSON {category, confidence}. On 300 hand-labelled tickets it agrees with human labels 91% of the time.
concepts.c: Why ask an LLM for JSON output and validate it, rather than parsing free text?
concepts.i: Expect to write a prompt for a data task, explain few-shot prompting, and describe how you'd check the output's quality.

concepts.title: Evaluating LLM outputs
concepts.kw: llm evaluation evals golden dataset llm as judge faithfulness groundedness relevance human review regression tests hallucination rate rubric
concepts.s: LLM outputs are open-ended, so evaluation needs test sets, clear criteria, and a mix of automatic checks, model-graded scoring and human review.
concepts.d: Build a golden dataset of realistic inputs with expected outputs or grading rubrics, including hard and edge cases. Use exact or programmatic checks where possible: valid JSON, correct labels, SQL that returns the right result. For open-ended answers, LLM-as-judge scores criteria such as faithfulness to sources, relevance and completeness against a rubric, but it must be validated against human ratings. For RAG, measure retrieval recall and answer groundedness separately. Run the eval suite on every prompt or model change as a regression test, and monitor production with sampling and user feedback.
concepts.e: Before switching models, a team runs 400 golden questions: the new model is cheaper and scores higher on relevance, but faithfulness falls from 96% to 89%, so they adjust the prompt before switching.
concepts.c: Why must an LLM-as-judge be checked against human ratings?
concepts.i: Senior roles ask how you'd evaluate an LLM feature before launch and keep quality from regressing.

concepts.title: Model deployment: batch and online
concepts.kw: model deployment batch scoring online inference real time api latency model serving containers canary shadow deployment model registry
concepts.s: A model only creates value once it's deployed. Batch scoring writes predictions on a schedule, while online serving answers requests in real time.
concepts.d: Batch scoring runs the model over many records on a schedule, such as nightly churn scores written to a table, and is simpler and cheaper. Online inference serves predictions through an API within a latency budget, such as fraud scoring in 50 milliseconds, and needs fresh features, scaling and high availability. Models are versioned in a model registry and packaged in containers with their dependencies. Release safely with shadow deployment (running the new model without acting on it), canary releases to a small share of traffic, or A/B tests, and keep a quick rollback path.
concepts.e: Churn scores are produced in a nightly batch job for the CRM, while the payment fraud model is served online behind an API and released by canary to 5% of traffic first.
concepts.c: When is batch scoring enough, and when do you need online inference?
concepts.i: Expect batch versus online trade-offs, serving architecture, and safe release strategies.

concepts.title: Model monitoring and drift
concepts.kw: model monitoring drift data drift concept drift prediction drift psi population stability index performance decay delayed labels alerts retraining
concepts.s: Models degrade after deployment as the world changes, so you monitor their inputs, outputs and performance and act before the damage builds up.
concepts.d: Data drift means input distributions change, such as a new customer segment or a changed upstream field. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and target changes, such as fraudsters adapting. Monitor input feature distributions with measures like the population stability index (PSI), prediction distributions, and data quality issues such as missing or out-of-range features. When labels arrive, often with a delay, track actual performance such as precision or MAE by segment. Set alerts and runbooks, and retrain on a schedule or when drift or performance thresholds are crossed.
concepts.e: A delivery ETA model's error rises 40% in July. Monitoring shows rain-related delays weren't in the training data's season, so it's retrained with monsoon data and a rainfall feature.
concepts.c: What's the difference between data drift and concept drift?
concepts.i: Expect what you'd monitor for a production model, how you detect drift, and how you decide when to retrain.

concepts.title: Experiment tracking with MLflow
concepts.kw: experiment tracking mlflow runs parameters metrics artifacts model registry reproducibility versioning weights and biases comparison
concepts.s: Experiment tracking records every training run's code version, data, parameters, metrics and outputs, so results can be compared and reproduced.
concepts.d: In MLflow, each run logs parameters (such as learning rate and depth), metrics (such as validation AUC, possibly per epoch), artefacts (plots, the trained model) and tags such as the Git commit and dataset version. Runs are grouped into experiments and compared in the UI to pick the best one. The model registry versions chosen models and moves them through stages such as staging and production, with approvals. Tracking the exact data version is as important as the code. Alternatives include Weights & Biases and the tracking built into cloud ML platforms.
concepts.e: Six months after launch, the team can see that the production churn model is run 4f2a: LightGBM, depth 6, trained on the March snapshot, validation AUC 0.84, at Git commit 9c1e.
concepts.c: Why log the dataset version as well as the code version for each run?
concepts.i: Expect how you track experiments, what you'd log, and how a model registry supports deployment.

concepts.title: ML pipelines and retraining
concepts.kw: ml pipelines training pipeline retraining automation feature pipeline validation gates champion challenger continuous training orchestration kubeflow sagemaker
concepts.s: An ML pipeline automates the path from data to a deployed model, so retraining is repeatable, tested and safe rather than a manual notebook exercise.
concepts.d: Typical steps: extract and validate data, build features, split, train, evaluate against the current production model and fixed thresholds, register the model, and deploy, each step orchestrated by tools like Airflow, Kubeflow or SageMaker Pipelines. Validation gates stop a bad model, for example one trained on a broken data load, from being promoted. Champion and challenger comparisons ensure the new model actually beats the current one. Retraining can run on a schedule or be triggered by drift. Everything is versioned, so any model can be traced back to its data and code.
concepts.e: A weekly pipeline retrains the demand model, checks the new data's row counts and nulls, backtests the challenger, and only promotes it if its WAPE beats the champion's by at least 1% on the last 8 weeks.
concepts.c: Why compare a newly trained model against the current production model before promoting it?
concepts.i: Senior MLOps interviews ask you to design a retraining pipeline with validation gates, versioning and rollback.

concepts.title: Causal inference and uplift modelling
concepts.kw: causal inference uplift modelling treatment effect heterogeneous effects t learner s learner propensity score persuadables incrementality targeting
concepts.s: Uplift modelling predicts how much an action, such as a discount, changes each customer's behaviour, so you target the people it actually persuades.
concepts.d: A normal response model predicts who will buy, but many of them would buy anyway. Uplift models estimate the treatment effect for each customer: the difference between their outcome with and without the action. Customers fall into four groups: persuadables (buy only if treated), sure things (buy anyway), lost causes (never buy) and sleeping dogs (react badly to being contacted). Methods include the T-learner (separate models for treated and control groups), the S-learner (one model with treatment as a feature) and uplift trees. They need randomised experiment data, or careful propensity score methods with observational data. Evaluate with uplift or Qini curves.
concepts.e: A coupon campaign targeted at the top 20% by uplift score generates 2.3 times the incremental orders of targeting the top 20% most likely buyers, because it skips customers who'd buy anyway.
concepts.c: Why is targeting the customers most likely to buy often a waste of a discount budget?
concepts.i: Senior data science roles in marketing and pricing ask how uplift differs from response modelling and how to evaluate it.

questions.q: Explain how a neural network learns.

p.t: Forward pass computes predictions and loss
Layers apply weights and non-linear activations
Backpropagation computes gradients with the chain rule

questions.a: In the forward pass, inputs flow through layers: each multiplies by weights, adds a bias and applies a non-linear activation such as ReLU, producing predictions and a loss. Backpropagation then computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight using the chain rule, working backwards through the layers. An optimiser like Adam uses the gradients to update the weights, and this repeats over many batches and epochs. Dropout, weight decay and early stopping help avoid overfitting.

questions.q: When would you use a neural network rather than gradient boosting?

p.t: Unstructured data like images, text and audio
Gradient boosting usually wins on tabular data
Neural networks need more data and tuning

questions.a: Neural networks shine on unstructured data like images, text and audio, where they learn features automatically, often starting from a pretrained model with transfer learning. On ordinary tabular data, gradient boosting usually wins: it's more accurate with less data and tuning, trains faster and is easier to interpret. Neural networks need more data and tuning, and cost more to train and serve. I'd also use them when I need learned embeddings or multi-task models.

questions.q: What are embeddings, and how are they used in data products?

p.t: Items as vectors where similar items are close

questions.a: An embedding represents an item, such as a sentence, product or user, as a vector of numbers, learned by a model so that similar items are close together, usually measured with cosine similarity. They power semantic search, recommendations, clustering, deduplication, and features for other models. They're stored in a vector database or a library like FAISS or pgvector, which runs fast nearest-neighbour search.

questions.q: How would you build semantic search over 1 million support articles?

p.t: Embed with one model for documents and queries
Evaluate with labelled queries and keep embeddings fresh

questions.a: Split articles into chunks of a few hundred tokens with titles as metadata. Embed every chunk, using the same embedding model for documents and queries. Store vectors in an approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW in a vector database, which searches a million items in milliseconds. Combine with keyword search in a hybrid setup, since exact terms like error codes matter, and rerank the top results. Evaluate with labelled queries using recall@k, and re-embed changed articles so the index stays fresh.

questions.q: Explain self-attention in a transformer.

p.t: Each token makes query, key and value vectors
Output is a weighted sum of values
Every token can attend to every other

questions.a: Each token's embedding is projected into a query, a key and a value vector. Comparing a token's query with the keys of all tokens, via scaled dot products and a softmax, gives attention weights: how much to focus on each token. The output for that token is a weighted sum of the value vectors. So every token can attend to every other token in the sequence, directly linking words far apart. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel, capturing several kinds of relationship.

questions.q: What's the difference between encoder models like BERT and decoder models like GPT?

p.t: Encoders read the whole text in both directions
Decoders generate one token at a time
Encoder-decoder models for translation and summarisation

questions.a: Encoder models like BERT read the whole text in both directions at once, so each token's representation uses context on both sides. They're good for classification, entity extraction and embeddings. Decoder models like GPT generate one token at a time and only see previous tokens, a causal mask, which suits text generation and chat. Encoder-decoder models like T5 combine both, encoding the input and generating an output, common for translation and summarisation.

questions.q: What are tokens and the context window, and why do they matter?

p.t: Cost and limits are measured in tokens
Context window is the maximum tokens per call
Long inputs must be chunked or summarised

questions.a: Tokens are the pieces of text a model reads, often part of a word; an English word is roughly 1.3 tokens. Cost is billed per token and speed depends on it too. The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can handle in one call, and it includes the prompt, any documents and the answer. So long inputs, like a year of support tickets, must be chunked, filtered or summarised first.

questions.q: Why do LLMs hallucinate, and how do you reduce it?

p.t: They generate plausible text, not look up facts
Instruct to say when unsure and cite

questions.a: LLMs predict the most plausible next token rather than looking up facts, so when they lack knowledge they still produce confident text. Their training data also has gaps or is outdated. To reduce it, ground answers with retrieved sources, as in RAG, so the model works from real documents or data. Instruct it to cite sources and say it doesn't know when the context lacks the answer. Use low temperature for factual tasks, and validate outputs, such as running generated SQL or checking numbers.

questions.q: Walk me through how a RAG system answers a question.

p.t: Documents are chunked and embedded into an index
Query is embedded and similar chunks retrieved
Hybrid search or reranking improves results
Chunks go into the prompt with instructions

questions.a: Beforehand, documents are chunked, embedded and stored in a vector index with metadata. When a question arrives, it's embedded and the most similar chunks are retrieved, often with hybrid search combining keywords, and a reranker picks the best few. Those chunks go into the prompt with instructions to answer only from them. The model answers and cites sources, so users can check, and access controls on documents carry through to what's retrieved.

questions.q: Your RAG assistant gives wrong answers. How do you diagnose it?

p.t: Separate retrieval failures from generation failures
Check whether the right chunks were retrieved
Check faithfulness to the retrieved context
Build an eval set of failing questions

questions.a: First separate retrieval failures from generation failures. For each wrong answer, check whether the right chunks were retrieved; if not, measure retrieval recall and fix chunking (too large or split mid-table), add metadata filters, use hybrid search or a reranker, or fix missing and stale documents. If the right chunks were there, the problem is generation: check whether the answer was faithful to the context, and tighten the prompt or try a stronger model. I'd turn the failures into an eval set to track fixes.

questions.q: How would you write a prompt to classify customer complaints with an LLM?
questions.a: State the task clearly with the allowed labels, such as six complaint categories, and a short definition of each, plus how to handle edge cases: an 'other' label, and choosing the main issue when there are several. Include few-shot examples of tricky tickets with the right label. Ask for structured JSON output with the category and a brief reason, and validate it in code. Then test on a labelled sample of a few hundred tickets, measuring agreement with human labels before running it on everything.

questions.q: How would you use an LLM to generate SQL safely and accurately?

p.t: Show the SQL to the user

questions.a: Give the model the relevant table schemas and column meanings, including business definitions like what counts as an active customer, plus example queries for common questions. Run the generated SQL with a read-only connection, row limits and timeouts, so it can't change data or run away. Validate the SQL by parsing it and checking it uses known tables, and check the results for sanity. Show the SQL to the user alongside the answer, so it's transparent and can be checked.

questions.q: How would you evaluate an LLM feature before launch?

p.t: Golden dataset of realistic and edge cases
Validate the judge with human ratings
Run on every change as regression tests

questions.a: Build a golden dataset of realistic inputs, including edge cases and known failure types, with expected outputs or grading criteria. Use programmatic checks where possible: valid JSON, correct labels, exact numbers. For open-ended outputs, use an LLM-as-judge with a clear rubric for faithfulness, relevance and tone, but validate the judge against human ratings on a sample. Then run the suite on every change to prompts or models as regression tests, and keep sampling production outputs after launch.

questions.q: What metrics would you use to evaluate a RAG system?
questions.a: For retrieval: recall or hit rate at k, meaning whether the chunks needed to answer were retrieved. For generation: faithfulness, also called groundedness, meaning every claim is supported by retrieved context, plus answer relevance and correctness against reference answers. Citation accuracy checks the cited sources really support the answer. Operationally, track latency, cost per query and user feedback such as thumbs up or down.

questions.q: Compare batch scoring and online inference for deploying a model.

p.t: Batch: scheduled predictions written to a table
Online: real-time API within a latency budget
Online needs fresh features and high availability
Choose by when the decision is made

questions.a: Batch scoring runs the model on a schedule, for example nightly, and writes predictions to a table for other systems; it's simpler and cheaper, and failures can be retried. Online inference serves predictions through an API in real time, within a latency budget such as 50 ms, and needs fresh features, autoscaling and high availability. I choose by when the decision is made: nightly churn scores for a CRM campaign can be batch, but fraud checks on a payment must happen in real time.

questions.q: How do you release a new model version safely?
questions.a: Register the new version in a model registry with its metrics and lineage. Run it in shadow deployment first: it scores live traffic but its predictions aren't used, so you compare it with the current model safely. Then a canary release to a small share of traffic, or an A/B test if you need to measure business impact. Monitor key metrics during the rollout, such as latency, prediction distribution and errors, and keep a fast rollback to the previous version.

questions.q: What would you monitor for a model in production?

p.t: Operational metrics like latency and errors

questions.a: Input data quality and distributions: missing values, out-of-range features and drift measured with PSI. The prediction distribution, since a sudden shift in scores often signals a problem before labels arrive. Performance once labels arrive, such as precision or MAE, tracked by segment like region or customer type. And operational metrics like latency, errors and throughput. Each gets thresholds, alerts and a runbook.

questions.q: What's the difference between data drift and concept drift, and how do you respond to each?

p.t: Concept drift: the input-target relationship changes
Detect data drift with PSI or distribution tests
Concept drift needs labels to detect

questions.a: Data drift means the input distributions change, for example more first-time users, while the patterns linking inputs to outcomes stay the same. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and target changes, like fraudsters adapting to the rules. Data drift can be detected immediately with PSI or distribution tests on features, but concept drift needs labels, shown by falling performance. For both, I'd investigate first, since drift can be a pipeline bug, then retrain on recent data, add new features, or change the model when the patterns have shifted.

questions.q: What would you log for each training run, and why?
questions.a: Parameters and hyperparameters, metrics on validation data (overall and by segment), the code version as a Git commit, and the data version, such as the snapshot date or dataset hash. Also artefacts such as the trained model, plots and feature importance, and the environment with library versions. That way any result can be compared and reproduced exactly, and when a production model misbehaves you can trace what it was trained on.

questions.q: What is a model registry, and how does it fit into deployment?

p.t: Links to the run, metrics and data
Stages such as staging and production
Deployment pulls a specific version and supports rollback

questions.a: A model registry is a versioned store of trained models, each linked to the run that produced it, with its metrics, parameters and data lineage. Models move through stages such as staging and production, with approvals and checks before promotion. Deployment pulls a specific version from the registry rather than a file from someone's laptop, so it's clear what's live, and rollback is just pointing back to the previous version.

questions.q: Design an automated retraining pipeline for a demand forecasting model.

p.t: Evaluate the challenger against the champion
Orchestration, schedule or drift trigger, and monitoring

questions.a: Steps: extract the latest data and run validation checks on row counts, nulls and freshness, stopping if they fail. Build features with the same code used in serving, then train. Evaluate the challenger against the current champion on a backtest over recent weeks. Only if it passes promotion gates, such as beating the champion by a margin with no segment much worse, register it and deploy. The whole thing is orchestrated in Airflow or a similar tool, runs on a schedule or a drift trigger, and is monitored like any pipeline.

questions.q: What can go wrong with automatic retraining, and how do you guard against it?

p.t: Training on bad or broken data
Feedback loops from the model's own decisions
Guards: validation gates, champion comparison, rollback

questions.a: It can train on bad data, like a broken load with half the rows, and a silently worse model gets promoted with nobody noticing. Feedback loops can form, where the model's own decisions shape its future training data, such as only seeing outcomes for approved loans. Training-serving skew appears if features are computed differently. The guards are data validation gates, comparing every challenger against the champion on a fixed backtest, segment-level checks, human approval for big changes, and a quick rollback.

questions.q: How is uplift modelling different from a normal response model?

p.t: Response models predict who will buy
Uplift predicts the change caused by the action
Persuadables, sure things, lost causes, sleeping dogs
Evaluate with uplift or Qini curves

questions.a: A response model predicts who will buy, but many of them would buy anyway, so a discount is wasted on them. Uplift predicts the change in behaviour caused by the action: the difference between buying with and without the offer. That separates persuadables, who buy only if treated, from sure things, lost causes and sleeping dogs, who react badly. Uplift models need data with treatment and control groups, ideally from a randomised experiment. They're evaluated with uplift or Qini curves rather than accuracy.

questions.q: Explain the T-learner and S-learner approaches to estimating treatment effects.

p.t: T-learner: separate models for treated and control
Effect is the difference in predictions
S-learner: one model with treatment as a feature
S-learner may ignore a weak treatment effect
Other methods like X-learner or causal forests

questions.a: The T-learner trains two separate models, one on treated customers and one on control, and estimates each customer's effect as the difference in predictions between the two models. The S-learner trains one model with treatment as a feature, then predicts each customer twice, with treatment on and off, and takes the difference. The S-learner may ignore a weak treatment effect if the model barely uses that feature, while the T-learner can be noisy with small groups. Other methods like the X-learner or causal forests address these weaknesses.
